title: Streamed JSON + Tool-Orchestration: Robust Parsing, Backpressure & Fallback Rules
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem statement: customers using streaming structured responses with tool/function calls observe brittle behavior when the model emits partial JSON, interleaves tool-invocation events, or when network backpressure truncates the stream. We need clear acceptance criteria and runtime behavior to guarantee deterministic assembly, predictable tool invocation semantics, and safe fallbacks so application developers can rely on streamed structured outputs for production workflows.
background: Multiple support tickets and internal incidents (INC-2026-44, INC-2026-59) show apps fail when the model emits an incomplete object mid-stream or when a tool call is signaled then the remainder of the schema does not arrive. Existing docs cover function-call contracts for non-streamed responses but are underspecified for streaming and interleaved events. This work clarifies: 1) how token-level stream chunks map to structured documents; 2) canonical backpressure/error modes; 3) semantics for tool invocation confirmation/cancellation in streaming contexts; 4) operational observability requirements for debugging partial outputs.
scope: In scope: streaming JSON (including arrays and nested objects), interleaved tool-invocation frames, error/fallback frames, SDK behaviors for reassembly, server-side auto-repair heuristics, and end-to-end tests. Out of scope: changing model fine-tuning, adding new low-level transport protocols beyond current SSE/HTTP/GRPC streams.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Streamed assembly: Given a valid model stream produced in 'structured-stream' mode, SDKs must be able to reassemble chunks into a single valid JSON document without requiring heuristic fixes. The runtime SHALL emit explicit 'stream_frame' metadata wrapper around structural tokens to preserve ordering (implementation detail).

2) Deterministic partials: If 'partial_object_mode' is enabled, each chunk must be syntactically valid JSON when interpreted as a fragment with a documented framing protocol. SDKs must provide APIs to access both incremental fragments and the currently assembled object state.

3) Tool invocation semantics: When the model signals a tool/function call during a stream, the runtime MUST deliver a single atomic tool_invocation event (id + payload). Tool_invocation events are authoritative and shall not be duplicated; any subsequent partial tool payloads are considered continuation of that invocation id. The runtime must provide a guaranteed until-finalized acknowledgement event for each tool call.

4) Backpressure and truncation: If network or runtime truncates a stream before the model emits a finalizing structural token, the runtime MUST produce a structured error object on the stream with keys 'error_type', 'partial_document', and 'recovery_suggestion'. 'error_type' must be one of ["truncated_stream","invalid_json","tool_call_incomplete"].

5) Auto-repair limits: Runtime auto-repair heuristics (closing brackets, injecting missing commas) are allowed only for 'repair_tolerance' <= 2 tokens missing and must be opt-in. Any auto-repair performed must be annotated in the final envelope with 'repaired': true and a short 'repair_summary'.

6) Fallback model: If a tool invocation cannot be executed because the tool payload is incomplete, runtime shall: a) mark the invocation as 'failed' with structured failure metadata, b) attempt model-level fallback (emit a recommended non-tool alternative response) if 'fallback_policy' is 'suggest', c) if configured, trigger a synchronous call to a fallback model variant. Acceptance tests must cover all three paths.

7) Observability: Streams must include token-level offsets and a per-stream unique 'stream_trace_id' that surfaces to logs, tracing, and console UIs. Console must show partial document previews and tool invocation timeline during the canary window.

8) SDK contract: SDKs (Node, Python, Go) must expose stable APIs: stream.on('fragment'), stream.on('assembled'), stream.on('tool_invocation'), stream.on('error'), and ensure that 'assembled' returns the same canonical JSON as the concatenation of fragments when no repair was applied.
9) Performance: Enabling 'structured-stream' must not increase median token latency by more than 8% for the same model/host configuration in dedicated runs (measured on runtime-1.26 benchmarks).

10) Security & privacy: Tool invocation payloads emitted over the stream must honor KMS/HSM encryption controls for dedicated/private deployments. Acceptance test will validate that sensitive fields are redacted in logs when sensitivity labels are present.
test_plan: Unit tests: fragment parsing, assembly, and auto-repair heuristics with synthetic truncated streams.
Integration tests: Node/Python SDKs reassembly tests with interleaved tool_invocation events; simulate truncation and verify structured error object formats and repair annotations.
E2E tests: Console shows partial previews, canary rollout against a subset of tenants, and coordinated failure injection (network cut) to validate 'truncated_stream' handling.
Load tests: measure additional latency and CPU overhead for structured-stream framing at 99th percentile under typical batching profiles.
Security tests: KMS integration test ensuring tool_invocation payloads are encrypted at rest and that logs redact PII according to sensitivity labels.
rollout_notes: Phase 1: Feature flag enablement for 'structured-stream' on staging clusters; SDKs default to off.
Phase 2: Canary to 5% of tenants with console preview enabled and additional tracing. Collect metrics for token latency, repair rate, tool-invocation success rate.
Phase 3: Gradual ramp to 50% if repair rate < 0.5% and tool invocation success rate > 99.5%.
Phase 4: GA with documentation, migration guide, and example patterns for common failure modes.
open_questions: 1) What is the canonical transport framing we commit to for long-term SDK compatibility? (SSE envelope vs gRPC framed messages)
2) Should we provide a default 'repair_policy' in hosted API or force customers to opt-in for auto-repair?

3) How do we handle multi-tool transactions where multiple tool_invocation events are generated in a single stream and some succeed while others fail? Do we provide a transaction id and rollback semantics?
4) Do we need an explicit 'finalize' token in the stream to disambiguate model-intent vs transport-close?
decisions: 1) We will require a stream_trace_id emitted at stream start for all structured streams. (Decided 2026-02-28)
2) Auto-repair will be opt-in and annotated; default is disabled for hosted API to avoid silent data corruption. (Decided 2026-03-02)
3) Tool invocations will be atomic events with a unique invocation_id and explicit finalization acknowledgement from the runtime. (Decided 2026-03-05)
4) Transport framing choice deferred: we will implement SSE envelope in runtime-1.26 and evaluate gRPC framing in next cycle. (Decided 2026-03-07)
